text: More than 2,500 years ago, the Mapuche already lived in the land that is now Chile.
Their name means “people of the land”, and they live in south-central Chile and south-western Argentina.
src: Archaeological finds show a Mapuche culture in Chile and Argentina as early as 600 to 500 BCE
Their name means “people of the land”, from mapu, “land”, and che, “person” / The Mapuche are an Indigenous people of south-central Chile and south-western Argentina

text: Most Mapuche were farmers who grew potatoes, maize and quinoa, and each family had a chief, the lonko.
A machi, usually a woman, is a healer who holds ceremonies to cure illness and to help the harvests.
src: Most Mapuche were farmers / The potato was the staple, especially in the south and on the coast where maize did not ripen, and they also grew quinoa / Each extended family was led by a lonko, or chief
the machi, a healer and spiritual specialist, usually a woman / The machi performs ceremonies to cure illness, ward off evil and influence the weather and harvests

text: About 475 years ago Spanish soldiers built forts on Mapuche land, and a war began that lasted nearly 350 years.
Leaders such as Lautaro won battles, and the land south of the Biobío River stayed free of Spanish rule.
src: From 1550 the Spanish built cities and forts in Mapuche lands / This began the Arauco War, a sporadic conflict of nearly 350 years
Lautaro built the first Mapuche cavalry and defeated and killed Valdivia at Tucapel / from 1598 kept their lands south of the Biobío River free of Spanish rule

text: Many Mapuche women still weave ponchos, blankets and belts, as their mothers and grandmothers taught them.
Mapuche silversmiths melted silver coins to make jewellery and headdresses.
src: Many Mapuche women still weave ponchos, blankets, bands and belts / mothers, grandmothers and aunts taught girls the techniques and the patterns of their locality
Mapuche silversmiths made their jewellery from melted Spanish, Argentine and Chilean silver coins / jewellery and coin headdresses called trarilonko

text: Later, Chile and Argentina took Mapuche lands by war, and thousands of Mapuche died.
Today they are the largest Indigenous people of Chile, and they still work for their land, language and rights.
src: Chile and Argentina conquered their lands between 1861 and the 1880s / Thousands of Mapuche died in combat, from pillage, starvation and smallpox
today the Mapuche are the largest Indigenous people of Chile and struggle for their land and rights / still press for their land, language and rights
